entry.dc:title: WHAT'S AHEAD FOR RUSSIAN MINING?
entry.dc:creator: Zaharlev G.
entry.dc:description: Future Soviet mining growth lies in expansion of surface mining which will provide 75-80% of total output by 1980.

entry.dc:title: Operational compliance with noise, blasting and dust controls
entry.dc:creator: Schaudies F.
entry.dc:description: Noise pollution control in the area of surface mining has been, up to the past year, a slowly developing science. It is, however, becoming a rapidly growing issue because of more rigid enforcement of the present noise standards set forth in the U.S. Federal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969. It is possible, and even probable, there will be an even greater degree of enforcement along with more stingent revisions of the present law. This paper examines some of the revisions that may have a great impact on operational compliance, particularly blasting and dust control.

entry.dc:title: Ecology and the problems of rehabilitating wastes from mineral extraction
entry.dc:creator: Goodman G.T.
entry.prism:publicationName: Proc Roy Soc London Ser A
entry.dc:description: With the growing demand for minerals in the United Kingdom, it is likely that there will be a marked increase in the area of land affected by deep and surface mining and associated industries, e.g. ore concentration plant, smelters. Improving technical knowledge of how to revegetate inexpensively, land disturbed by mining helps to ensure that mineral extraction is not inhibited by nor necessarily inhibitory to other valid uses for land. Revegetation is important because experienced experienced planners have found in practice that revegetation appears to restore to a derelict or disturbed site the greatest flexibility of potential re use for the widest range of subsequent developments. Traditionally, three approaches approaches to revegetation appear to have been used: accept site conditions as they are, and plant with species known to tolerate harsh conditions, e.g. ecological 'pioneer' species; improve the soil as a medium for plant growth by incorporating, for example, NPK fertilizer, lime and organic matter; use geological knowledge to pre plan excavations so that toxic wastes are buried below the rooting zone. A combination of all three seems most desirable and involves careful species selection together with predictive physicochemical physicochemical analysis of those site conditions which which may inhibit plant growth.

entry.dc:title: IN WEST VIRGINIA HILLS. . . IT'S HAULBACK MINING ALL THE WAY.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: This Princess Susan coal mine of Charleston, W. Va. operation is an excellent example of surface mining performed together with reclamation work, in natural sequence and without spoil pushed over the hill or highwalls left behind.

entry.dc:title: IMPACT OF THE RAILROAD INDUSTRY ON MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Graves T.
entry.dc:description: As a case-in-point of the impact of a modern, well organized transportation of coal by rail over long distances by means of unit trains on the economics of surface mining, the boom in the Wyoming's mining industry is described. Coal activity on the Union Pacific is currently centered around the once near ghost town of Hanna, Wy. The coal rush along Union pacific Railroad lines in this area actually began taking on boom proportions in 1972 with the start up of a new strip mining operation, expansion of another mine and the addition of five new unit train operations. Today, the rich coal fields of Wyoming are being tapped to serve the elejctric utilities for boiler fuel hundreds of miles eastward from the nearby Continental Divide.

entry.dc:title: WANTED: NEW SYSTEMS FOR SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Michaelson S.
entry.dc:description: Recent and current productivity trends in US surface mining are discouraging: they show the industry to be noncompetitive in comparison with other industries both in the US and abroad. Extensive research on productivity and costs, as witnessed in the US nonferrous, metallic surface mines, shows that on the average 10% of cost if attributable to breaking rock, 16% for shovel loading, and close to 45% is accounted for by ore and overburden haulage. The average industry-wide stripping ratio is estimated at about 2:1. Obviously, then, the stripping ratio (3 tons moved for 1 ton of ore) has the greatest potential for improving the productivity and reducing ore cost. The next, greatest target for productivity improvement is the haulage system. Paper discusses potential techniques in that direction.

entry.dc:title: MATERIALS IMPROVEMENTS IN SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT.
entry.dc:creator: Weston W.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The four basic material requirements for mining equipment are suggested by the authors who then proceed to discuss some of the ways these requirements are met by improved materials, with particular reference to surface mining equipment. A review of excavating and drilling machinery is given along with developments in design. Foreign inclusions in the material are singled out as the biggest single problem resulting in a substantial reduction in the physical properties of the steel used in surface mining equipment.

entry.dc:title: Determination of an Economic Size of a Producing Facility. Theoretical Fundamentals, Influence on Costs, Practical Application to a Surface Mining Operation.
entry.dc:creator: Kellermeyer W.
entry.dc:description: Success of an industrial operation is determined by its proper size and parameters such as productivity of the crew, productive facilities, raw materials, as well as planning, organization, and management. The theoretical fundamentals are examined and their application is illustrated on the example of a complex, surface mining operation.

entry.dc:title: UNIQUE APPROACH TO GET OIL SHALE OUT OF THE GROUND.
entry.dc:creator: Smith C.
entry.dc:description: Paper describes the geology of the Piceance Creek Basin, Colo. , oil shale deposit and presents a proposed surface mining system after partial removal of the overburden. Theoretical financial calculation for production of 500,000 bpd is included.

entry.dc:title: NEW USES FOR BUCKETWHEEL EXCAVATORS.
entry.dc:creator: Griffin T.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining today is faced with a twin challenge: accelerating the rate of removal of massive quantities of overburden and ore; and replacing comparable high volumes of overburden in the mined-out portion of the pit. It is against this background, coupled with increased demands for fossil fuels worldwide and legitimate environmental concerns, that the role of bucketwheel excavators and reclaimers has been raised to new prominence. As an innovative use that may mean low cost and a high volume article describes the application of bucketwheel excavators for removal of overburden and mining of an ore deposit with simultaneous replacement of overburden in the exploited parts of the open pit.

entry.dc:title: ADVANCES IN HARD ROCK MINING - ACHIEVEMENTS AND EXPECTATIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Janelid I.
entry.dc:description: Paper analyzes the importance of rock excavation in world wide, underground and surface mining of ores and industrial minerals. The pertinent statistics show that the ratios of the volume of rock excavated in underground and surface mining to the volume of ore were 1 to 5 and 1 to 1,1 respectively. Impact of rock excavation on the total costs of mining necessitates intensive research and development work in areas of: drilling; drifting and raising; rock drills; blasting; loading and transportation; as well as in rock mechanics. Recent Scandinavian achievements are reviewed.

entry.dc:title: Reclamation in steep slope surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Hamilton L.
entry.dc:description: Today's complex methods of mining coal on the steep slopes require millions of dollars of equipment and precise timing in order to maintain production and protect the environment. Recently, the West Virginia Department of Natural Resources established some administrative guidelines that would make steep slope operations comply with proposed U.S. requirements. This new steep slope mining theory has been labeled 'controlled placement' of spoil. Controlled placement involves the placement of spoil in steep areas where its condition can be completely stabilized and revegetated. This covers the head of the valley fill, mountain top removal, haulback, over the shoulder, block cut and any other methods where the overburden is technically delivered, hauled or compacted so that there are no adverse after effects when mining has been completed. This paper further describes the application of this technique to steep slope mining and discusses some of the results that have been obtained to date.

entry.dc:title: RECLAMATION PROBLEMS IN SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Grandt A.
entry.dc:description: Paper discusses the reclamation of surfaced mined coal lands in the Unites States in the 1970's from several aspects, namely, reclamation requirements, policies and techniques. In particular the legislation in effect, topsoiling, grading, water supplies, and climate are examined.

entry.dc:title: OPEN PIT URANIUM MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Graves J.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining at Anaconda's Jackpile-Paguate mine, located between Albuquerque and Grants, N. M. , begins with the delineation of the ore bodies through surface drilling and geophysical probing. Assay information is fed into a computer for the determination of ore-to-low grade for reserve calculation purposes, and the blocked-out areas are mined using conventional blasting, stripping, and loading techniques.

entry.dc:title: TRANSPORTATION FOR COAL.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Comprehensive study of various techniques for coal transportation is divided into following chapters: mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic options in deep-mine transport; haulage trucks for carry coal in surface mining; overland conveying, inclusive of coal-slurry pipeling; railroad-transportation; and using waterways to ship coal.

entry.dc:title: Inspiration's design for clean air. I
entry.dc:creator: Dayton S.
entry.dc:description: A detailed description of the major design and operating factors involved in the Inspiration Consolidated Copper Co.'s new $54 million electric smelter and double absorption sulfuric acid plant are presented in this first of a two part article. The new plants, which both contain some of the largest componentry of their type anywhere, are expected to yield many benefits in spite of their high cost. The smelter, equipped with a Norwegian Elkem 51 mva furnace and five Belgian siphon converters of Hoboken Overpelt design, started phasing into the production line in May 1974 as a replacement for an older, reverberatory, Pierce Smith converter installation handling a green charge. Coupled to the new smelter (which handles 1,500 tpd of copper concentrates and copper precipitates of Inspiration and toll origin) is a 'showcase' 1,330 tpd Lurgi acid train fed from an elaborate collection system that 'dry cleans and launders' electric furnace and siphon converter offgases. The new project places Inspiration first among western US copper smelters in the race to meet the Environmental Protection Agency's 90% sulfur recovery goal for stationary plants. The replacement system will enable mothballing of the present smelter as a reserve asset. The major topics of discussion are: How Inspiration settled on the new system; fitting the new facilities to the existing system; about the world's largest electric copper furnace; the enriched exit gas dividend; slag and matte tapping; sealing of the siphon convertors; how copper conversion is handled; gas handling; cold gas cleaning; making acid in a quality plant; and waste heat recovery in the steam plant. The second part of this series will present a profile of Inspiration mining and processing from ore to finished copper rod.

entry.dc:title: OIL SHALE: A SOLUTION TO THE ROADBLOCK.
entry.dc:creator: Livingston C.
entry.dc:description: The roadblock to development of United States oil shale resources is neither technology nor economics. Rather, the central issue is the fact that an area as vast as that underlain by the Green River Formation of Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming simply cannot be developed by using conventional concepts of mine layout. The problem is not one of developing a single oil shale mine or even a series of oil shale mines. Rather it is one of developing the natural resources of a vast area encompassing sodium and aluminum minerals, natural gas, water resources, land, and forests, as well as oil shale. Paper critically reviews the three approaches to the oil shale development that are being pursued, to wit: underground mining; in situ retorting; and conventional surface mining. A new proposed complex technique that should be planned on a regional basis and which is described in detail, would encompass; a new blasting technology, mining method and layout; materials handling systems; as well as a method for land reclamation and water resource development.

entry.dc:title: LAND REHABILITATION: PROMPT PASSAGE OF FEDERAL RECLAMATION LAW RECOMMENDED BY FORD FOUNDATION STUDY.
entry.dc:creator: Box T.
entry.dc:description: No issue associated with the current energy debate is more in the center of conflict between exploitation and conservation than is the surface mining of coal. Indeed, restoration of a landscape disturbed by surface mining, in the sense of duplicating former conditions, is not possible. In order to avoid the confusion caused by the vague terminology, the panel on surface mining of the National Academy of Sciences has issued following definitions: ″Restoration″ implies that the conditions of the site at the time of disturbance will be duplicated after the action. ″Reclamation″ implies that the site is habitable to organisms that were originally present, or others that approximate the original inhabitants. ″Rehabilitation″ as used in this report implies that the land will be returned to a form and productivity in conformity with a prior land use plan including a stable ecological state that does not contribute substantially to environmental deterioration and is consistent with surrounding aesthetic values. In light of the above definitions, special ecological problems of western coal lands, relationship of surface mining to environment, and recommendations for rehabilitating western land are discussed.

entry.dc:title: ARIZONA: COAL MOVES ON NATION'S FIRST 50-kv ELECTRIC RAILROAD.
entry.dc:creator: Bellas R.
entry.dc:description: Arizona's most extensive proved coal reserves are in the northeastern part of the state in Black Mesa, a 3200-sq mi area in portions of Apache, Navajo and Coconino Counties. Proved reserves, established by Peabody Coal Co which in the mid-1960s began exploration in the area are considered to be approximately 2 billion tons. One of the operating units, the Kayenta mine has coal deposits similar to those at the adjacent Black Mesa mine, and the surface mining methods are similar. Two pits are now worked. Diesel-electric haulers move the coal from the pits to a 2700-tph conveyor which feeds the coal to two 1000-tph crushers. The 2-in. size product is taken from a storage hopper and loaded onto a three-flight conveyor system which carries the coal 6 one-half mi across the mesa to storage silos at the railroad loading point. The Black Mesa & Lake Powell Railroad, built by International Engineering Co, Inc, a subsidiary of the Morrison-Knudson Co, was built expressly for this mining operation and is completely automated. Each train comprises three electric locomotives pulling 73 cars, each of 122-ton capacity. There are three train trips daily, six days a week, with non-stop unloading at the generating station. An engineer rides the train only to prevent a possible malfunction of electronic controls.

entry.dc:title: WYOMING: PRODUCTION SEEN DOUBLING BY 1976.
entry.dc:creator: Glass G.
entry.dc:description: Wyoming's coal industry is rapidly emerging from its depression era of the late 1950s. The sharpest upturn in production began in 1969 and shows no sign of stopping. From that year, production tripled from 4. 6 million tons annually to 13. 6 million tons in 1973. Because production forecasts cannot keep pace with recent developments, it is only safe to say that Wyoming coal mining activity is accelerating at unprecedented rates and that surface mining accounts for most increases in annual tonnage. Coal-related developments and existing and proposed mines within Wyoming are shown on state's map. Efforts of the individual mining companies are described. Developments in coal gasification are outlined.

entry.dc:title: NEW MEXICO: STATE STILL BOASTS NATION'S LARGEST SURFACE COAL MINE.
entry.dc:creator: Bellas R.
entry.dc:description: History of the development by the Utah International, Inc (UI) of the Navajo surface mine in the Four Corners area of New Mexico is briefly described. The leases covering 31,000 acres are estimated to contain a minimum of 1. 1-billion tons of coal. The coal seams lie 10 to 120 ft beneath the surface. Coal grade averages between 9000 and 10,000 Btu, and the sulfur content is about 0. 6%. Ash varies on the high side, about 18-20%, but the disposal problem is simplified by a short haulback to the pit area, where the ash is buried. The mine which uses conventional surface mining methods is producing 25,000 tpd of coal. Mining activities of other companies are described.

entry.dc:title: NORTH DAKOTA: PROPOSED COAL GASIFICATION COMPLEX WILL TAP LIGNITE RESERVES.
entry.dc:creator: Conrad C.
entry.dc:description: Under present plans the state's four existing coal-fired generating plants, having a capacity of 750 Mw, will eventually be increased to 2320 Mw. Estimated coal consumption of these four expanded plants will be 27. 1 million tons of coal annually. Biggest news in the history of the North Dakota lignite industry was approval on Feb 19 1974, of a plan to divert 17,000 acre-feet of water annually from Lake Sakakawea for a coal gasification plant. The lake lies north of the Garrison Dam on the Missouri River. Michigan Wisconsin Pipe Line Co of Detroit was given the go-ahead for one plant, although three have been proposed. Construction of the plant, costing up to 500 million, is expected to begin in 1979. The North American Coal Corp will supply 10 million tpy of coal for gasification which would, on the average, require surface mining 800 acres annually. Based on an estimated plant life of 30 years, this would require surface mining 24,000 acres, compared with the total of 7000 acres surface-mined in the state since records were first kept in 1884. Michigan Wisconsin will build the plant using the Lurgi gasification process. North Dakota gas will be carried by a pipeline extending across North Dakota from Alaska. The Nordth Dakota lignite has more than a 30% water content - 2% on the surface - and a heat value of about 6800 Btu per lb. In comparison, subbituminous coal yields about 9000 Btu per lb. (North Dakota's coal deposits are exclusively lignite. )

entry.dc:title: An aerial-photographic analysis of the environmental impact of clay mining in New Jersey
entry.dc:creator: Garofalo D.
entry.dc:description: Black and white, color and color-infrared photography at 1:20,000 scale or larger provide useful data for monitoring the environmental effects of surface mining as demonstrated following a study of surface clay mining in New Jersey. Investigations using high-altitude color and color-infrared photography at scales of 1:80,000 to 1:120,000 provide an efficient technique for inventorying large-surface mining operations or for rapid statewide mining studies. © 1974.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINE OF THE FUTURE.
entry.dc:creator: Cornforth C.
entry.dc:description: If the industry is not all but abolished under federal legislation, a fantastic, exciting future is ahead for surface mining, particularly in the West. To accomplish that goal even larger, than presently available, excavators (boom-, and bucket wheel type) tractors, scrapers, and motor trucks will be needed, source of which are described. Techniques for land reclamations are discussed.

entry.dc:title: Digging into mine waste
entry.dc:description: In the U.S., mining activities now affect approximately 13 million acres, or about 0.5% of the total U.S. land area. Of this total, 7 million have been undercut, 3 million disturbed by surface mining, and 3 million given over to mining related waste accumulations. The subject of mining related environmental pollution is discussed and some of the possible remedial measures for the reparation of environmental damage are considered. Because of aquifer and stream disruption, both coal and hard rock mines give rise to water pollution from mine drainage, both acid and alkaline. The polluting effects of solid waste production through disposal of mine tailing after mineral values are extracted, such as land slides, air pollution through dust blowoff, and smoldering from spontaneous combustion, are also discussed. Some of the more effective methods of restoring environmental damage and meeting Federal pollution control standards are reviewed.
